findings.issue_text: **`packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:96`** — `prisma` is used (`await prisma.credential.update(...)`) but never imported anywhere in this file (compare to the removed diff: no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` was added). Every call to `getClient()` — i.e. every Salesforce calendar operation, since it's invoked from the constructor — will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime. This breaks the Salesforce integration entirely, not just the sync feature. Fix: add `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma";`.
**`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:5-9`** — The "minimum" schema used in sync mode is broken:

**`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:25-27`** — When `refresh_token` is missing from the (already-stripped, per #2) response, the code sets it to the literal string `"refresh_token"`:

This placeholder value gets persisted directly into `credential.key.refresh_token` in the DB (see `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:96-99`, `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:265-272`), permanently corrupting the credential with a bogus, non-functional refresh token. Fix: don't fabricate a fake token — either keep the previous `refresh_token` (merge, don't overwrite) or throw/skip the update.

**`packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:93-95`** — `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw `fetch` `Response` object in sync mode (`refreshOAuthTokens.ts:291-298`, just `return response`), but the non-sync path returns `fetchTokens.res`, a gaxios response with a `.data` property. The caller does `const token = res?.data; googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token;` — in sync mode `res.data` is `undefined` (raw `Response` has no `.data`), so `token.access_token` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. This is caught by the surrounding `try/catch` (line ~99-111) but silently swallowed with no logging, and the token is never refreshed — Google Calendar sync silently breaks whenever `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is configured.

**`packages/app-store/hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:192,202`** — Same shape mismatch as #4: in sync mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw `fetch` `Response`, but the caller treats it as a `HubspotToken` (`hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn * 1000)` → `NaN` since `expiresIn` is `undefined`; `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken)` → `undefined`). Unlike #4, this doesn't throw — it silently persists a corrupted credential (`expiryDate: NaN`, `accessToken: undefined`) to the DB via `prisma.credential.update` at line ~194-199. This is worse than a crash because it's undetected data corruption.

**`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:60-65`** — Webhook secret comparison uses `!==` instead of a constant-time comparison (`crypto.timingSafeEqual`). This endpoint can create/overwrite arbitrary users' app credentials given a valid secret, so a timing side-channel on secret verification is a meaningful risk for a security-sensitive endpoint. Also `req.headers[...]` can be `string[]` (duplicate headers), which would always fail comparison — not a security hole, but worth normalizing.

**`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:31`** — `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws on invalid input instead of using `safeParse`/try-catch, so malformed requests get an unhandled exception → framework 500 (potentially leaking stack details) rather than a clean 400. Other API routes in the codebase use `defaultResponder`/`defaultHandler` for consistent error handling; this endpoint doesn't follow that convention.

**`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62-71`** — `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId: appMetadata.slug } })` picks an arbitrary existing credential to overwrite when a user has multiple credentials of the same app type (e.g. multiple connected Google Calendar accounts, which Cal.com supports). There's no way to disambiguate which credential to update, so this can silently overwrite the wrong account's credentials for users with multiple connections to the same app.

**`packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:75-99`** — Unlike every other provider touched in this PR, Salesforce's token refresh is (a) unconditional — it refreshes on *every* `getClient()` call (i.e. every service construction) rather than only when the token is near expiry, causing an extra network round-trip to Salesforce on every calendar operation and needless refresh-token rotation; and (b) not routed through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so Salesforce doesn't participate in the credential-sync feature this PR is adding, unlike Google/Office365/Hubspot/Lark/Webex/MSTeams. This is an inconsistent, incomplete application of the stated PR goal.

**`packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:86`** — `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw ...` is a fragile way to detect failure; `statusText` is not guaranteed to be the string `"OK"` across environments/proxies. Should check `response.ok` or `response.status === 200`.

**`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/createOAuthAppCredential.ts:164-191`** — The team-credential branch checks only that the user is an *accepted member* of the team, while the personal-credential branch calls `throwIfNotHaveAdminAccessToTeam`. This is an inconsistent authorization check: any regular team member (not just team admins/owners) can install an OAuth app credential for the whole team by driving the OAuth flow with a crafted `teamId` in state, while the same user would be blocked from doing so via the non-team path check. Worth confirming this is intentional; if not, apply the same admin check in both branches.

**`packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:262-264`** — The previous `console.error` logging of the zod parse error and raw MS response on refresh failure was removed (now `parseRefreshTokenResponse` just throws a generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" with no context). This is a debuggability regression for diagnosing OAuth refresh failures in production. Also, since `parseRefreshTokenResponse` now throws on failure rather than returning a `safeParse`-like result, `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` at line 264 is dead code (always true if reached).

**`packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/api/add.ts:17`** — `` `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback` `` is now a template literal with no interpolation (should just be a plain string); also this change (hardcoding vs. using `appConfig.slug`) is unrelated to the OAuth-sync PR intent and adds unexplained scope creep.

No tests were added for any of the new OAuth utilities (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`, `createOAuthAppCredential`, the webhook handler) despite them containing the exact logic bugs found above (#2-#5) — unit tests around the schema-stripping behavior or the sync-mode response shape would have caught these before merge.

`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` has no rate limiting; combined with #6 (non-constant-time secret comparison), this modestly increases brute-force exposure for an endpoint with credential-write power, though 32-byte secret entropy makes this low practical risk.

goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: **`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:5-9`** — The "minimum" schema used in sync mode is broken:

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `minimumTokenResponseSchema`, the object shape uses computed keys like `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. Those expressions evaluate to a single literal string key (whatever `toString()` returns for the Zod schema object), not “any string key”. That means the schema does **not** actually accept arbitrary numeric expiry fields / arbitrary extra properties as intended, and the second computed key likely overwrites the first if they stringify the same. In Zod the correct way would be `.catchall(...)`, `.passthrough()`, or a `z.record(...)`/intersection. So the “minimum schema” is indeed broken in the diff.

Therefore, in `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` the new code `const tokenResponse = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema);` will only return when `tokenResponse.success === true`. That makes the subsequent merge `...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data)` effectively redundant/always `tokenResponse.data` if reached, matching the finding’s “dead code” claim.

Also, the diff removes the prior `console.error("Outlook error grabbing new tokens ...", tokenResponse.error, "MS response:", responseJson)` block, and the thrown error from `parseRefreshTokenResponse` is generic and carries no zod/MS-response context. That is a verifiable loss of diagnostic information compared to the previous behavior in this file.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No tests were added for any of the new OAuth utilities (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`, `createOAuthAppCredential`, the webhook handler) despite them containing the exact logic bugs found above (#2-#5) — unit tests around the schema-stripping behavior or the sync-mode response shape would have caught these before merge.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add new OAuth utilities and a new webhook handler, and it does not include any accompanying test files/changes. However, the proposed finding frames this as a concrete defect (“exact logic bugs found above (#2-#5)”) and asserts tests would have caught them—those referenced bugs are not shown in this diff, and there is no project requirement in the diff mandating tests for new code. So while ‘no tests added’ is observable, it’s not a verifiable correctness/security defect introduced by this diff, and the “would have caught” claim is speculative.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` has no rate limiting; combined with #6 (non-constant-time secret comparison), this modestly increases brute-force exposure for an endpoint with credential-write power, though 32-byte secret entropy makes this low practical risk.

adjudication.rationale: The new webhook endpoint `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` performs a secret check using a simple `!==` comparison and then allows credential create/update in the database. There is no rate limiting, throttling, or lockout logic in this handler before the secret check (or anywhere else in the file), so repeated requests could be used to brute-force the header value. While the secret is intended to be high-entropy, the absence of rate limiting on a credential-write endpoint is a verifiable security hardening gap introduced by this diff.
